subject: research/marriage-divorce-evidence
professional: a demographer or survival-analysis statistician who publishes on union dissolution from NSFG/NLSY data (would check the weighting and censoring, the first-marriage denominator, held-out calibration, and whether a risk calculator overstates what a C of about 0.66 can say)

evidence.correctness: Recomputed three outputs from sources other than the author's code. (1) From the committed extract app/train/nsfg_pooled_women.json.gz (n 29,202, 10,529 events, weights mean 1.0, matching the README's 'fitted on NSFG first marriages' counts) I ran my own weighted Kaplan-Meier in numpy: cumulative dissolution 4.87% at 1y, 20.89% at 5y, 33.37% at 10y, 48.32% at 20y; the project's weighted_survival.csv gives 1-0.6673 = 33.27% at 10y and 1-0.5178 = 48.22% at 20y (0.1 point apart, ties handling), and the published NCHS value (Copen et al. 2012, NHSR 49, women, 2006-2010) is about 20% at 5y and 32-33% at 10y. (2) competingRisks() in app/mortality.js with a constant 1.5% divorce hazard, a woman of 28 and a man of 30 married in 2027, 50 years: node gives divorce 0.472750004, widowhood 0.238200981, still married 0.289049012; an independent Python reimplementation from the raw UN mx table gave 0.47275000364506015, 0.2382009833278769, 0.28904901302706315 (agree to 1e-15). (3) BA-by-wedding subgroup KM at 10y from the extract: 37.6% (no degree), 36.4% (some college/associate), 15.3% (BA+), which agrees in direction and size with the README's lower risk for the degree couple (7.4/12.5/19.1% at 5/10/20y for a typical engaged couple, a model value I could not reproduce without re-running the fit, but 12.5% at 10y is below the BA+ raw 15.3% as expected when other protective traits are added). A fourth check was inconclusive: a period life table from the 2024 UN female mx row gives e0 about 82.4 (my approximation, ages 0-14 assumed 1% mortality), against my recollection of about 81.5 for the UN; the file stores ages 15-100 only so the claimed e0 check (0.02 years) cannot be recomputed from the committed file. Not run: the model refits from raw NSFG/NLSY files, because the raw data are not committed and several GB.
evidence.completeness: Checked claimed items: calculator (app/) runs under 40 node test files, 158 tests; seven lenses (NSFG pooled, NLSY97, NLSY79, SIPP, Canada GSS, NSFG 2002, ACS) each have a model bundle and test vectors in app/models; reproducibility/ has 65 folders with METHODS.md and SHA256SUMS; literature evidence (286 records, export of 10 to the app) present; Report.html, report-app and MODEL_CARD.md present. Not end to end: the reproducibility scripts need data that the repository does not hold (downloads from NCHS, BLS, Census, Stanford; restore_inputs.py is the only file in scripts/), so I could not rerun any refit; NEXT.md (2026-10-20) lists open work the author itself says users would notice first (extended race, family-of-origin, religion, occupation inputs not in the form, guided decision flow). The README's headline (3.4% Poisson loss reduction) refers to the NLSY79 couple panel while the 'Try it' paragraph reports a different default model (NSFG pooled, C 0.661): two headline models in one README.
evidence.verification: Ran python3 -m pytest test_*.py: 84 passed, 2 skipped (skips are tests that need absent data). Ran node --test tests/*.test.mjs in app/: 158 pass, 0 fail. The train test reproduces scikit-learn GLM coefficients to 3.6e-14 and held-out loss to 3 decimals (additive spline 5.688% vs 5.688%, tree 3.333%), and a Python reference is used for competing risks. Seeded mutation: in app/mortality.js changed 'const h = hd + ha + hb;' to 'const h = hd + ha;' (drops the spouse's mortality). Result: 3 failures out of 158 (per-lens scoring, lenses.test.mjs, 'competing risks match Python on every test couple'). Reverted with git checkout; git status clean for the subject. Weakness: most test vectors are generated by the author's own pipeline, but the sklearn and Python cross-implementations are independent code.
evidence.craft: Read app/mortality.js (clean, hazards documented, edge clamp on age and year), app/index.html footer, README.md, MODEL_CARD.md, NEXT.md, METHODS.md excerpts, and listed app/*.js sizes (7,721 lines; lens-adapters.js 1,347, couple.js 959, app.js 685). Defects: README.md carries two '**Live page:**' lines, the second to an external chatgpt.site host (a leftover from the first author tool, the Report.html also tests for .chatgpt.site); MODEL_CARD.md has missing spaces in generated numbers ('40,818intervals/5,735respondents', 'older1957–1964'); mortality tables are clamped silently outside 15-100 and the table years (documented in code, not surfaced to the user); scripts/ holds one file while the analysis code is spread across 65 reproducibility folders with their own requirements, so no single entry point rebuilds the headline.
evidence.claims: Checked: 'C 0.661' for the default model against reproducibility/nsfg_pooled_first_marriage/heldout_model_comparison.csv (additive_2002features_pooled harrell_c 0.661411, CI 0.6548-0.6702): backed. '3.4% loss reduction' vs constant: backed by MODEL_CARD and the NLSY79 panel and, for NSFG, improvement_over_duration_only 3.38%. '43,336 NSFG marriages' (women plus men, 29,202 + 14,134 = 43,336 per weighted_survival.csv): backed. Disclaimers: 'Not advice of any kind' in app/index.html; MODEL_CARD 'Use' paragraph warns against optimizing a prospective spouse; Canada over-prediction 1.7x disclosed in README. Weak points: the example 'typical engaged couple' is at the '2nd percentile' of NSFG risk, which is by definition not typical (wording contradicts itself); the README's best held-out model (additive_spline C 0.695 in the same CSV) is not the app default, and the reader is not told why; the title 'will your marriage last?' for an instrument with C about 0.66 is stronger than the MODEL_CARD's 'no validated individual forecast'.
evidence.fitness: A researcher could build on it: public-use data only with SHA256 checksums, CIs from design-based replicate weights, person-held-out folds, a committed 29,202-row browser extract, bundles with test vectors, and an honest model comparison showing flexible models do not beat additive ones. Nearest prior work: Copen et al. 2012 and Bramlett and Mosher 2002 (NCHS life tables, parsed and cross-checked here), Raley and Bumpass 2003, Karney and Bradbury (2020) reviews, and Lyngstad and Jalovaara's union-dissolution reviews; the new contribution is harmonised cross-survey validation (NSFG to NLSY97, SIPP, Canada) and a decision-aid layer. It is not a paper: there is no manuscript with a named venue, no comparison against a published risk model, and Report.html is a report rather than an article. A researcher cannot rerun the fits without redownloading roughly 10 GB of files.
evidence.domain: Compared against standard union-dissolution demography (Cox or discrete-time hazard on first marriages, NCHS weights, right censoring at interview, duration-based life tables). It matches: first marriages only, weights, person-held-out folds, competing mortality, Poisson/piecewise rates. Departures a demographer would flag: separation and divorce are pooled as 'dissolution' in NSFG but legal divorce in NLSY79; women-only extract for the training lens, men scored by symmetric averaging; independent deaths between spouses (disclosed in the mortality notes); cross-period drift (wedding_year in the model) means extrapolation to couples marrying today relies on a trend; the Canada level miss (1.7x) shows weak transport across populations. Individual-level discrimination is modest (C 0.66, 10-year AUC 0.656), and the presentation of a single risk percentage needs the interval displayed beside it.

defects.what: Headline example is described as a 'typical engaged couple' but sits at the 2nd percentile of NSFG first-marriage risk (median 10-year risk 28% vs 12.5%); a reader will take 7.4% / 12.5% / 19.1% as the typical case.
Default calculator model (C 0.661) is not the best held-out model in the project's own table (additive_spline C 0.695); the reason for the choice is not stated beside the headline.

No single script rebuilds the headline: raw data are not committed, scripts/ has one file, 65 reproducibility folders each have their own steps, and the committed life-expectancy check cannot be recomputed from the committed table (ages 15-100 only).
Two 'Live page' lines in the README; the second points to an external chatgpt.site host.
MODEL_CARD.md numbers run into words without spaces ('40,818intervals/5,735respondents').

verdict: A large, careful, honestly caveated research and calculator project on public survey data. Independent recomputation (my own weighted Kaplan-Meier from the committed extract, a Python reimplementation of the competing-risks engine) matches the project's numbers and published NCHS values. Tests are strong: 84 Python and 158 node tests pass, include scikit-learn parity to 1e-14, and a seeded mutation that dropped the spouse's mortality term was caught by 3 tests. It is not a finished paper (no manuscript or named venue) and a researcher cannot rerun the fits without redownloading the raw files. Wording defects: the 'typical couple' example is a 2nd-percentile couple, and the default model is not the best held-out one. The 3 scored at the bar for correctness, claims and verification (4), median 3.
